extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars and patent litigation practitioners (judges, lawyers, policymakers) interested in injunction practice
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical and doctrinal analysis of factors that influence whether U.S. district courts grant permanent injunctions in patent litigation after eBay, including case characteristics, patentee type, technology field, and forum effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable harm (first eBay factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-eBay patentees must demonstrate irreparable harm before an injunction can issue; prior to eBay irreparable harm was often presumed when validity and continuing infringement were clearly established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts identify specific types of irreparable harm (loss of market share, price erosion, loss of goodwill, loss of future business opportunities, inability to pay, other). In the dataset, loss of market share was the most common basis (80%). The article codes findings on irreparable harm as a binary variable and reports statistical significance of differences across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate remedy at law (second eBay factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether damages (monetary relief) are an adequate remedy; this inquiry 'inevitably overlaps' with irreparable harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In 136 decisions where a court found irreparable harm it also found no adequate remedy at law in all but one case; conversely, when courts found no irreparable injury they also generally found an adequate remedy at law. Courts often treat these two factors as collapsing into a single inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of hardships (third eBay factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the balance of hardships between patentee and infringer favors granting an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where injunctions were denied, courts found the balance of hardships weighed against an injunction in about 50% of denials (30 of 60). Examples include findings that an injunction would cause massive job losses or large investments to be lost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest (fourth eBay factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether granting an injunction would be contrary to the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public interest weighed against an injunction in slightly over half of denial cases (52%; 31 of 60). Courts frequently deny injunctions in medical-device cases where removal from market could harm patients or eliminate important alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal nexus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The asserted irreparable harm must be causally connected to the infringement (i.e., a 'causal nexus' between the patented technology and the harm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have denied injunctions where the patented technology was not causally connected to the alleged irreparable harm; several post-study decisions also denied injunctive relief for lack of causal nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of market share (type of irreparable harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Loss of market share, including lost customers and lost sales, due to infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded as a binary variable [MKTSHARE]. Most common basis for finding irreparable harm (80% of injunction cases). Often tied to cases where parties are market competitors; courts view lost market share as difficult to remedy with money damages in many circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price erosion (type of irreparable harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Price erosion for the patentee's product or services that practice the patent (reduced ability to charge premium price).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded as [PRICE]. Observed in ~13% of injunction decisions. Price erosion is competition-related and can be treated as irreparable because it may be hard to fully compensate later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of goodwill or reputation (type of irreparable harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Damage to the patentee's brand, reputation, or customer goodwill due to infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded as [GOODWILL]. Found in ~43% of injunction decisions. Courts treat goodwill as often difficult to quantify, making it a common basis for irreparable-harm findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss of future business opportunities (type of irreparable harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lost prospective business, licensing opportunities, or future contracts as a result of infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded as [FUTUREBUS]. Observed in ~19% of injunction decisions and treated as a competition-related harm that can support irreparable-injury findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inability to pay monetary judgment (type of irreparable harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Risk that the infringer would be unable to satisfy a money judgment, making damages inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded as [INABILITY]. A less common basis (~5%) for irreparable-harm findings; typically occurs when a large monetary judgment would render the infringer insolvent and leave the patentee uncompensated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other irreparable harms (type of irreparable harm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other harms not captured by the main categories, such as loss of qualified employees, diversion of R&D funds, loss of revenue from other licensees, impairment of patent market value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coded as [OTHER]. Occurred infrequently (~17%) but included a variety of harms courts sometimes find difficult to compensate with money damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee identity / PAE status
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee is a patent assertion entity (PAE) or another type of patent holder affects injunction outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This study classifies patentees into categories (e.g., Large Patent Aggregator; Failed Operating or Start-Up Company; Patent Holding Company; Technology Development Company) and aggregates to a binary PAE variable. Universities and individual inventors were excluded from the PAE category. PAEs rarely obtained permanent injunctions after prevailing on liability (16% for PAEs vs 80% for other patentees); differences were statistically significant (p < 0.001). Exceptions occur when a PAE previously attempted commercialization (failed operating company) and can show irreparable harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition between litigants
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patentee and infringer are market competitors is a major predictor of injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitor patentees received injunctions in the overwhelming majority of cases (84%; 150 of 179), while non-competitors rarely succeeded (21%; 8 of 39). Courts often grant injunctions to keep an infringing competitor out of the market, though specific sectors (e.g., medical devices) may be denied for other eBay reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small component / 'component' consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patent covers a small component of the accused product (as opposed to a core element) influences courts to be reluctant to issue an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following concerns about holdup (Justice Kennedy's concurrence), cases where the patented feature is only a small component of a larger product are negatively correlated with injunctions. The regression models show highly significant negative odds ratios for the COMPONENT variable (.06, .04, .02 across models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing behavior (offer to license or license history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the patent holder licensed or offered to license the patents-in-suit is considered when evaluating equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a variable [LICENSE] in regression analysis and anticipated to be negatively correlated with injunctive relief; courts consider prior licensing conduct in assessing the adequacy of monetary remedies and equitable posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-method patent status
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the asserted patent claims a business method is a case characteristic hypothesized to affect injunction likelihood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as [BUSMETHOD] in regression models and anticipated to be negatively correlated with injunctions; business-method patents are commonly asserted by PAEs and may be associated with lower injunctive relief rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A finding of willful infringement is expected to increase the likelihood of injunctive relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as variable [WILLFUL] in regression models and anticipated to have a positive association with entry of a permanent injunction (i.e., odds ratio > 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The technological field of the patents-in-suit (software, electronics, electrical, mechanical, chemistry, drugs, medical device, biotechnology) affects injunction probabilities and must be controlled for in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biotechnology was omitted from some models because it had a perfect predictive rate (injunctions granted in all biotech cases in the dataset). Field-of-technology controls are important because PAE activity and injunctive outcomes vary by technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue / district effects
rubrics_metrics.description: District court and forum choice influence injunction outcomes; some districts have substantially higher grant rates than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 2 reports injunction grant rates by district (e.g., District of New Jersey 92%, District of Massachusetts 82%, Central District of California 73%, National average 72.5%, Eastern District of Texas 61%, Northern District of California 60%, District of Delaware 50%). Regression Model #3 controls for the six districts with the most injunction decisions. Venue selection and local norms/practices are significant predictors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance and multiple testing adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of statistical tests (Pearson’s chi-square) to compare grant rates and application of multiple testing penalties (Bonferroni adjustment) when assessing significance across multiple categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study reports p-values (e.g., p = 0.004, p = 0.006, p < 0.001) and notes results remained significant after Bonferroni adjustments across technology categories or districts. Researchers should adjust for multiple comparisons when testing many categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression modeling and interpretation (logistic regression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing the impact of multiple factors on injunction decisions using logistic (logit) regression, reporting odds ratios, standard errors, significance levels, and pseudo-R2 as model-fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Odds ratios > 1 indicate positive association with injunction entry; < 1 indicate negative. Significance indicated by * (p<0.05), ** (p<0.01), *** (p<0.001). Pseudo-R2 values reported (.31, .37, .45) indicate predictive power; models should control for technology and district effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change in presumption post-eBay
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrinal shift after eBay: courts no longer presume irreparable harm; patentees must prove irreparable injury and inadequacy of monetary remedies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrinal change is central to post-eBay injunction analysis and explains why courts now conduct detailed factual findings on types of harm and adequacy of remedies. Historical context and case examples (pre- and post-eBay) illustrate the shift.
